outcome: No proof, disproof or AI-attributed result on whether every nonnegative integer appears has appeared since 26 January 2024; the only in-window events are a February 2026 OEIS computation that pushed the smallest missing value check to 10^612 terms with 852655 still missing, and OEIS variant entries about record-index structure, neither of which moves the question.
problem_asks: One yes/no question: does every nonnegative integer occur as a term of Recamán's sequence? The sequence is a(0)=0 and, for n>=1, a(n)=a(n-1)-n if that value is nonnegative and not already a term, otherwise a(n)=a(n-1)+n. Part 1 (only part): surjectivity onto the nonnegative integers. Because a(0)=0 and every term is nonnegative, 'every nonnegative integer' and 'every positive integer' are the same question, so the January 2024 wording and the wording in some later sources are equivalent. The smallest value not yet seen (852655 = 5*31*5501) is an instance of this question, not a separate part. Wikipedia's wording: 'Neil Sloane has conjectured that every number eventually appears, but this has not been proven.'

events.what_happened: Allan Wilks computed the first 10^15 terms of A005132 and reported (OEIS comment dated 6 Nov 2001) that all numbers below 852655 had appeared, while 852655 = 5*31*5501 was missing. The OEIS EXTENSIONS section also carries an undated, unattributed note 'After 10^15 terms of A005132, the smallest missing number was 852655.' This is a finite computation reported in the OEIS entry, not a paper.
events.delivers: Finite check: among the first 10^15 terms, every value below 852655 occurs and 852655 does not. Says nothing about whether 852655 or any larger integer ever occurs.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks: the universal claim that every nonnegative integer occurs is untouched.
events.directly_checkable: The rule is fully specified and can be re-run from a(0)=0 to any stated index; a re-run would reproduce the finite statement but cannot establish non-occurrence of any value.
events.direction: Neutral on surjectivity: computational evidence that the first missing value is large, which fits either that every value eventually appears or that some never do.

events.what_happened: Benjamin Chaffin posted a series of OEIS A005132 comments extending the finite search, each stating that 852655 is still the smallest missing number: 10^25 terms (13 Jun 2006); 7.78*10^37 terms (28 Mar 2008); 4.28*10^73 terms (22 Mar 2010); and 10^230 terms (dated 2018 only, year precision). Each is a finite computation reported in the OEIS entry.
events.revisions: Later comments in the same OEIS entry: 28 Mar 2008, 22 Mar 2010, 2018 (10^230), and 8 Feb 2026 (see chaffin-computation-2026).
events.delivers: Finite checks up to the stated index: 852655 still missing at each stage. Nothing about the universal claim.
events.directly_checkable: As for wilks-2001-computation: reproducible by re-running the rule to a stated index; finite and so cannot settle the universal claim.
events.direction: Neutral on surjectivity: each stage pushes the search further while leaving the smallest missing value unchanged.

events.what_happened: OEIS A005132 comment by Benjamin Chaffin dated 25 Jan 2018 lists the first 13 missing values as of that date: 852655, 930058, 930557, 964420, 966052, 966727, 969194, 971330, 971626, 971866, 972275, 972827, 976367.
events.delivers: A list of values not yet seen as of that search depth. Establishes that there are many missing values in the computed range; does not establish any of them is never attained.
events.directly_checkable: The listed values can be checked by re-running the rule to a depth past each value's position.

events.what_happened: Alekseyev, Myers, Schroeppel, Shannon, Sloane and Zimmermann, 'Three Cousins of Recamán's Sequence', arXiv:2004.14000 (v1 29 Apr 2020; v2 3 Jun 2021), published in Fibonacci Quarterly 60(3) (2022), 201-219, DOI 10.1080/00150517.2022.12427470. The paper defines three new sequences A(n), B(n), C(n) built from n, and its introduction restates the original Recamán question as open. Per search snippets (not verified in the PDF, which I could not read), it says the most basic question, whether every nonnegative integer appears, is still unanswered, and that 852655 is still missing after the 10^230-term computation.
events.revisions: v1 29 Apr 2020; v2 3 Jun 2021 (current); journal version Fibonacci Quart. 60:3 (2022), 201-219.
events.delivers: On the original sequence: nothing; it restates the question as open. On the cousins (a different question): an upper bound A(n) <= n^2-2n-1 (per search snippet); a conjectured asymptotic for B(n); and C(44)=2783191412912 computed, with termination of the C(n) search unproved.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: the paper does not settle surjectivity of the original sequence.

checked_by.qualification: Peer-reviewed journal publication in number theory / combinatorics; referee identities not public.
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in 2022. I did not verify the refereeing process, and the publication concerns the cousin sequences, not the original question.

events.directly_checkable: The cousin sequences are computable from their stated definitions; the paper reports the C(44) value, which can be checked by direct computation.
events.doubts: The paper does not attempt to settle the original question, so it is a restatement, not a claim. Its cousin results are about different sequences and do not bear on surjectivity.
events.direction: Restates the original question as open; its own results cut neither way on it.

events.what_happened: N. J. A. Sloane, 'A Handbook of Integer Sequences' Fifty Years Later, arXiv:2301.03149 (v1 9 Jan 2023; v2 16 Jan 2023), section 4.1 on A005132. The section states the main question, 'Does every positive number appear?' (the word is 'positive'), records 'Thirty years ago I thought that every number would eventually appear' and 'Now I am not so sure', reports that 852655 was the smallest missing number and that 'there has been no progress since then', and lists 'Open question: Does 852655 appear in A005132?'. It gives two possibilities: infinitely many numbers never appear, or every number eventually appears but may not be reachable.
events.delivers: A survey restatement, not a result. Establishes the author's stated uncertainty about surjectivity and that the 852655 instance remained open as of January 2023.
events.doubts: Survey statements of belief by the sequence's own curator are opinion, not evidence for either side of the question.
events.direction: Opinion shifting toward 'infinitely many missing terms' but explicitly not a proof; leaves surjectivity open.

events.what_happened: N. J. A. Sloane talk 'The Reluctance of a Sequence' (Rutgers, May 2024), slides hosted at sites.math.rutgers.edu/~zeilberg/EM24/projects/sloaneGF.pdf. Per a search snippet, the slides say that after 10^230 terms 852655 is still missing, and that Sloane now thinks there are infinitely many missing terms with 852655 the first of many. I did not open the slides (the file exceeded the fetch size limit), so the date and the 'infinitely many' wording are from the snippet only.
events.delivers: No new mathematics claimed in what I could see. Reports the state of the computation and the author's opinion; establishes nothing about surjectivity.
events.doubts: Content known only from a search snippet; the slides were not read.
events.direction: Opinion leaning toward non-surjectivity, not a result in either direction.

events.what_happened: Benjamin Chaffin comment on OEIS A005132, dated 8 Feb 2026: 'Even after 10^612 terms, the smallest missing number is still 852655' (the EXTENSIONS section of the fetched page carries the same statement without 'Even'). This is a finite extension of the same search. The Wikipedia article (last edited 16 Sep 2026) says 'As of 2026, 10612 terms have been calculated', which is presumably 10^612 with the superscript lost in extraction. This event is in the window and is the only new computational event I found after January 2024.
events.delivers: Finite check: 852655 still missing after the stated number of terms. Establishes nothing on the universal claim.
events.directly_checkable: The computation is reproducible from the rule for any stated depth; again finite, so it cannot settle the universal question.
events.doubts: The 10^612 comment was read through a summarising fetch of the OEIS page; I did not read the raw page text. A separate OEIS entry (A392407, see chaffin-A392407-2026) carries a 10^612 figure with a different meaning, and a search summary attributed the 10^612 figure to that entry, so the attribution should be checked against the raw A005132 page.
events.direction: Neutral on surjectivity: pushes the finite search further without changing the smallest missing value.

events.what_happened: OEIS A392407 by Benjamin Chaffin, submitted 9 Feb 2026: indices n at which the sequence reaches a record run of consecutive subtraction steps (first indices 4 and 111; R(111)=40 after three consecutive subtractions). The comments include a(14) > 10^612 as a bound on a record index.
events.delivers: About a structural record in the sequence's up/down pattern, and a lower bound on a record index. Nothing about which integers occur.
events.directly_checkable: Record indices can be checked by direct computation of the sequence to the stated index.

events.what_happened: OEIS A393814 by Benjamin Chaffin, submitted 28 Feb 2026: 'Minimum value taken by Recamán's sequence (A005132) between terms where A005132(k) mod k increases.' A search snippet says its comment identifies these points as the places where the sequence has the best chance of filling in a small missing number. The fetched entry page gave the name and a b-file link (n = 1..5104), not the comment text.
events.revisions: Entry marked as last modified 10 Mar 2026 per a search snippet, not verified.
events.delivers: A structural observation about where minima occur in the sequence; not a result that any given integer appears or fails to appear.
events.directly_checkable: Minima can be recomputed from the rule to the stated index range.
events.doubts: The 'best chance' remark is a heuristic observation in an OEIS comment, not an argument.

summary: I ran 42 web searches (listed below) and opened the Wikipedia article, the OEIS entries A005132, A064228, A392407, A393814, the arXiv abstracts 2004.14000, 2301.03149 (plus its HTML v2), 2608.11941, 2605.22763 and 2601.11757, the Sloane-hosted and DeepMind repository pages, and the SeqFan post. The sequence (OEIS A005132, contributed by Bernardo Recamán Santos in 1991) is still listed as open in every source I could read. Wikipedia says Sloane 'has conjectured that every number eventually appears, but this has not been proven'. The 2023 Handbook section 4.1 lists 'Does 852655 appear in A005132?' as open with no progress since 2018, and the 2020 'Three Cousins' paper (arXiv 2004.14000, Fibonacci Quarterly 2022) restates the question as open while proving results about different cousin sequences. The only in-window events are computational: Chaffin's OEIS comment of 8 Feb 2026 reports the smallest missing value still 852655 after 10^612 terms, which is one more finite check on a universal claim and moves nothing under section 2.1, and two OEIS variant entries (A392407, A393814) on record-index structure that do not bear on surjectivity. Sloane's stated view has moved from expecting every number to appear ('thirty years ago' in the 2023 Handbook, i.e. around 1993) through 'not so sure' (OEIS, 26 Feb 2017, per the A005132 page) to a 2023 two-possibility survey and a May 2024 talk that reportedly favours infinitely many missing terms; these are opinions, not results. Close calls: (a) Whether the 2026 computation or the 2024 talk should be recorded as events at all; I recorded both, with the reason they move nothing. (b) Positive versus nonnegative: since a(0)=0, the two wordings are equivalent, so I did not treat the change as a scope shift. (c) Wikipedia's '10612 terms' is presumably 10^612 with the superscript lost, which matches the 2026 OEIS comment. (d) The 10^612 attribution: the OEIS A005132 page as read through a summarising fetch carries it, while a search summary attributed it to A392407, which only has a bound a(14) > 10^612; I could not check the raw page, so this is recorded in doubts. On AI involvement: none of the AI searches (AlphaEvolve, GPT-5, DeepMind/OpenAI/Anthropic, LLM proof, FrontierMath, Erdős-problem AI results, ML pattern search, AI-assisted OEIS, Lean formalisation) connects any system to this sequence, so none_found is true for every event. That depends on one open lead. Tsoukalas et al. (arXiv 2605.22763, submitted 21 May 2026, v2 8 Jun 2026) report AlphaProof Nexus 'proved 44/492 OEIS conjectures'; Adamczewski (arXiv 2608.11941, 12 Aug 2026) reports LMs resolving 147 of the same 492 open OEIS conjectures, and his SeqFan post of 24 Aug 2026 gives 160 settled. I could not establish whether any A005132 conjecture is in those 492 or was settled: the tadamcz.com explorer renders only a title without JavaScript, the GitHub directory listings are partial, and the guessed file paths FormalConjectures/OEIS/5132.lean, oeis_5132_conjecture_0.lean, A005132.lean and oeis_A005132_conjecture_0.lean all returned 404. If A005132 is among the 492 and a model settled it, that would be a new event with its own AI record and would need adding; I did not find evidence of one. Not found: a Lagarias-Rubinstein density result, which I half-recalled but could not locate, so I do not record it.
competing_reading: One could read the 2023 and 2024 statements by the sequence's curator, together with the finite computations, as evidence that the answer is no (infinitely many values never appear), which would make this a case of the problem leaning negative. But these are beliefs, and no argument or counterexample is offered; a counterexample would need an exhibited missing value shown never to occur, which nobody has produced. A second reading treats 852655 itself as the question: a proof that 852655 appears would then look like a resolution. Under problem_asks it is one instance of a universal claim, so it would not settle the problem, and the record should not count it as settling.
what_would_settle_it: A proof that every nonnegative integer occurs in A005132, or a proof that some specific value (for instance 852655), or infinitely many values, never occur. Failing that: a dated update to OEIS A005132 or the Handbook section 4.1 changing the open status; the arXiv listings for 'Recamán' in math.NT from 2024 onward; and a check of whether A005132 (or the Recamán sequence under another name) is one of the 492 OEIS conjectures in arXiv 2605.22763 / 2608.11941 and, if so, its settlement status with its AI record.

incomplete: (1) Rutgers 'The Reluctance of a Sequence' slides (sloaneGF.pdf) not opened: file exceeded the fetch size limit. The May 2024 date and the 'infinitely many missing terms' wording come from search snippets only. (2) arXiv 2004.14000 PDF and Fibonacci Quarterly Sloane PDF could not be read with my tools (binary streams); the 'most basic question still unanswered' sentence and the 'A(n) <= n^2-2n-1' result come from search snippets, not verified text. (3) The 10^612 comment on OEIS A005132 was read through a summarising fetch; the raw page was not read directly, and a search summary attributed the 10^612 figure to A392407 instead. (4) Membership of A005132 in the 492 OEIS conjectures used by Tsoukalas et al. (arXiv 2605.22763) and Adamczewski (arXiv 2608.11941) is unverified: the OEIS Open explorer renders no entries without JavaScript, the arXiv PDFs were unreadable, and the GitHub listings are partial; the four guessed Lean file paths for A005132 returned 404. If A005132 is in the set and was settled by a model, that would be an additional event to add. (5) The Handbook text of section 4.1 was read through a summarising fetch of the HTML v2, so the quotations are as extracted, not checked against the PDF. (6) The date of the 2017 'not so sure' comment (26 Feb 2017, from the A005132 Comments section) is recorded in the summary only, not as an event, since it is an opinion. (7) Not checked: OEIS entry history for A005132 (to see if any AI-assisted submission exists), the Numberphile 2018 video, and Google Scholar citation lists for arXiv 2004.14000 and 2301.03149.

judgement.why: Every event is either a finite computation of the sequence (instances: a search to 10^N terms leaves the universal question untouched, and 852655 being unseen is not shown to be never attained), a survey/talk restating the question and an opinion (none), structural OEIS entries about record indices and minima (none), or results on different 'cousin' sequences (variant). Nothing proves surjectivity or exhibits a provably missing value. No AI system is credited in any event. The pre-2024 computations are marked checkable since the rule is explicit and re-runnable at modest depths, though for the astronomically deep runs this is moot; they are discarded as instances either way.
judgement.doubts: The researcher could not determine whether A005132 is among the 492 OEIS conjectures in the AlphaProof Nexus (arXiv 2605.22763) and OEIS Open (arXiv 2608.11941) studies; if one was settled by a model it would be an unrecorded event, though an OEIS 'conjecture' there would more likely concern a side property than the famous surjectivity question. The 2024 talk content is from a snippet only, and the 10^612 attribution to A005132 vs A392407 is unconfirmed; neither affects the answers.
